items.title: Sailing along a constant compass bearing draws a spiral around the pole
items.claim: A 'rhumb line' (loxodrome) is a path that crosses every meridian at the same angle — what you sail if you hold a constant compass course. Except for due east/west (the equator) or due north/south, a rhumb line spirals around the pole, eventually reaching it after infinite winding.
items.prompt: Why doesn't a constant bearing give a great circle?

options.text: Great circles change bearing as you traverse them (except along the equator or meridians); to maintain a constant compass bearing, you must follow a different curve that spirals — the loxodrome
It only happens near the pole

items.reveal:
A loxodrome (rhumb line) is the curve that intersects all meridians at the same angle. On a sphere, this is an equiangular spiral.

For any constant bearing not aligned with the equator or a meridian, the path spirals around the pole. The length to reach the pole is finite (the spiral converges) but the number of windings is infinite.

On a Mercator projection, rhumb lines appear as straight lines — this is the property Mercator designed his projection for in 1569. Hold a ruler against a Mercator chart and you have a constant compass bearing course.

Great circles, by contrast, appear as curves on Mercator maps, generally bowed toward the nearer pole. Modern aviation uses great-circle routes; old-school open-ocean sailing used rhumb lines (easier to navigate without constant heading recalculation).

In practice: long-distance navigation often combines them — fly an approximate great circle, but compute waypoints at intervals (e.g., every 5 degrees of longitude) and sail rhumb lines between waypoints. This is 'composite sailing'.

The loxodrome was first studied by the Portuguese navigator Pedro Nunes (1537). It contributed to the systematic mathematisation of navigation in the Age of Discovery.
items.why: Compasses point to magnetic north. Holding a constant bearing draws a curve that no Euclidean intuition prepares you for — and the difference between loxodrome and great circle has shaped maps, navigation, and naval strategy for centuries.

items.title: Computers compute sine by adding up polynomials
items.claim: Your calculator can't 'compute sine'. It computes a polynomial that approximates sine very accurately. Specifically, sin(x) = x - x^3/6 + x^5/120 - x^7/5040 + ... The Taylor series gives any function as a sum of polynomial terms.

options.text: Polynomials and sine are always equal
Any analytic function f(x) can be expressed as a power series sum of f^(n)(a) * (x-a)^n / n!; truncating to a few terms gives a polynomial approximation with rigorously bounded error near x = a
Only sine has a Taylor series

items.reveal:
Taylor series: f(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + f''(a)(x-a)^2/2! + f'''(a)(x-a)^3/3! + ...

For analytic functions (most functions arising in physics and engineering), the series converges to f(x) within a radius of convergence around a.

Key examples around a = 0 (Maclaurin):
sin(x) = x - x^3/3! + x^5/5! - x^7/7! + ... (converges for all real x)
cos(x) = 1 - x^2/2! + x^4/4! - x^6/6! + ... (converges for all real x)
e^x = 1 + x + x^2/2! + x^3/3! + ... (converges for all real x)
ln(1+x) = x - x^2/2 + x^3/3 - ... (converges for |x| < 1)
1/(1-x) = 1 + x + x^2 + x^3 + ... (converges for |x| < 1, geometric)

For small x, truncating after a few terms gives good approximation. For sin(x), keeping x - x^3/6 gives error of about x^5/120; for x = 0.1, error ~ 10^(-8).

Calculators use TWO TRICKS:
1. Argument reduction: reduce sin(x) for large x to sin(x') where x' is in a small range, using periodicity and symmetries.
2. Polynomial approximation: minimax polynomials (Chebyshev-optimal) often beat Taylor for fixed precision.

Applications:
- Computer hardware (FPUs): implement transcendental functions via polynomial approximation.
- Numerical analysis: many algorithms (Newton-Raphson, Runge-Kutta) involve Taylor expansion.
- Physics: small-angle approximations (sin x ≈ x, cos x ≈ 1) are first-order Taylor.
- Perturbation theory in quantum mechanics: expansion of solutions around exactly-solvable cases.

Divergent Taylor series: some functions have Taylor series that converge only at a single point (formal series that don't represent the function). These appear in asymptotic analysis (Stirling's approximation, certain physics calculations).
items.why: Functions like sine seem 'analytical' or special. Computationally, they're polynomial approximations. The Taylor expansion is the practical universal interface between abstract functions and computers.

items.title: 45 degrees is only optimal for a projectile in a vacuum
items.claim: Every physics textbook says the maximum range for a projectile is at launch angle 45 degrees. True in vacuum. In real air, the optimum angle is significantly less — and for some launches it's barely above 30 degrees.
items.prompt: Why does air change the optimum?

options.text: It doesn't — 45 degrees is always optimal
Air resistance reduces both horizontal velocity and vertical velocity, but the loss to drag is greater on long airborne paths; lowering the angle reduces flight time and total drag exposure
Gravity is different at high angles

items.reveal:
Vacuum case: range = (v^2 / g) * sin(2 * theta). Maximised at theta = 45 degrees.

With linear drag (low-speed air): the optimum angle decreases with launch speed and drag coefficient. For a thrown baseball or shot put, optimum is ~42-43 degrees.

With quadratic drag (more realistic at high speed): for a golf ball, optimum is closer to 12-15 degrees (combined with backspin for lift). For an artillery shell, often 30-40 degrees due to high muzzle velocity and dense air.

Why: higher launch angles mean longer flight times, more time exposed to drag, more total energy lost. The trade-off between vertical reach and drag loss shifts the optimum downward.

For a long-jumper, who launches around 7-10 m/s, the optimum angle calculated from biomechanics is ~22 degrees, not 45 — because the long-jumper cannot achieve high vertical velocity from horizontal sprint and because air resistance is minor. Body-mechanics constraints matter more than the equation.

The 45° result is a useful first approximation but should not be taken as universal. Most real-world projectile design uses computational fluid dynamics rather than analytical formulas.
items.why: Textbook results assume ideal conditions. In real applications (golf, baseball, artillery, athletics), the answer is shifted — often substantially — by drag and biomechanical constraints. 'Theoretically 45°' is correct for nothing on Earth.
